A realm worth learning.

How Vạn Thắng — Ten Thousand Victories can become comfortable, compelling mobile strategy while rewarding deep desktop play.

Main mode: Dragon AscentMobile + desktopEvidence-led design review48 prioritized backlog items

The strongest next move is to make existing depth easier to use.

Preserve the realm economy, personal histories and formation combat. Give players clearer consequences, quieter preparation and a satisfying victory milestone. Add new mechanics only where they create a different plan—not simply more actions.

01

Keep the identity

Đông Hồ art, Vietnamese characters and a living court distinguish this game. Connect that identity to terrain, commitments and tactical situations.

02

Reward preparation

Show how a farm, commander, treaty or reinforcement changes the coming fight. Audit whether escalating prices and threats preserve the benefit of playing well.

03

Offer a complete reign

A short charter can end in triumph. Players can bank it, choose a harder chapter, or carry a strong build into Endless.

This is a design assessment, not a claim about human retention or commercial success. Scores are editorial judgments with stated evidence. Recommendations and numerical acceptance targets are proposals to validate.

02 / UNDERSTANDING THE GAME

The game already contains a substantial strategy system.

The main menu’s primary mode is Dragon Ascent: a single-player real-time grand-strategy roguelite. It combines a procedural realm, automated or manual administration, escalating invasions, live tactical encounters and an inherited dynasty. Skirmish offers isolated combat. Older empire/campaign/rival code remains accessible to development hooks but is shelved from the normal menu; it is not counted as a shipped main-mode feature.

Shape the realmDoctrine, provincial focus, construction, court, claims and diplomacy.
Prepare for invasionRead incoming pressure, position hosts, fund defence and preserve supply.
Command or delegateFormation, stance, stamina, moments, reinforcement and withdrawal.
Recover and inheritLosses, rewards, more waves; defeat eventually banks progression.

TerritoryA generated 42-province realm; loyalty, claims, travel and connected supply. Six claim methods: bribe, diplomacy, intimidation, settle, occupy and siege.Compare route value and readiness at contact. Make loyalty, acquisition time and success chance distinct in the decision.

ProgressionLegacy perks/loadout, Dynasty traits/lineage, Cabinet collection and combinations, plus cosmetics and codex discovery.One clear inheritance explanation and normalized challenges. Prefer additional choices over more compulsory stat accumulation.
Comfort systemsContextual Copilot, strategic pause, a separate battle pause, saves, resume, offline support, phone controls and a dedicated desktop layout.Audit consistency and device performance; do not rebuild features that already exist.

The clock matters

A strategic tick is 3.5 seconds. The first invasion is scheduled after 16 ticks, about 56 simulation seconds, with a nominal 14-tick interval thereafter. Prompts pause the strategic clock, so those values do not predict a person’s session length.

The first three waves are constrained opening columns. Great invasions occur every four waves. Relations, pressure and battle state modify the experienced rhythm.

Desktop is a different default

Normal desktop entry enables Hands-on: autopilot and routine lane prompts are disabled. A headless state factory leaves this off. A wide screenshot alone is therefore not a desktop gameplay test.

The desktop checks here explicitly used ?layout=desktop and confirmed ascent.hardcore === true after normal menu entry.

Primary code map: menu defaults, timing and balance constants, run lifecycle, card pool, desktop controls.

03 / DIRECT PLAY & OBSERVATIONS

I played the decisions, then checked their consequences.

A fresh mobile-profile run entered through the real menu. I explored coronation, named and crowned a ruler, read the empty inheritance screen, chose the Granaries boon, selected a hero bringing neighbouring land, appointed a treasurer, chose Fortify, changed provincial focus, attempted a bribe and chose Salt Roads. The bribe failed and reduced trust; the report explicitly explained why. The realm later repelled its first invasion, with a named commander and 46 friendly losses in the inspected aftermath.

That sequence demonstrated both real agency and attention cost. Before I could settle into map planning, doctrine, province, expansion, draft, invasion response, law, envoy and court decisions repeatedly took the screen. The detailed coronation path was my choice: “Let the chroniclers decide” already provides a shortcut. This is not evidence that every player must complete all customization steps.

What the play sessions establish—and what they do not
  • Direct strategy play: one new mobile-profile reign through the first repelled invasion and the next wave’s opening, with screenshots and JSON state; an isolated equal-army Skirmish ended in a rout.
  • Desktop: normal menu entry confirmed Hands-on; setup choices were then advanced through the existing UI event path to inspect map planning. Native keyboard/mouse inputs opened Build, selected a defensive focus and opened Army.
  • Focused combat check: a separate instrumented 9,000 vs 9,000 Skirmish accepted native formation and stance inputs. The saved control log confirms Shields and Press took effect by round 5; the pause then held round and troop counts unchanged. No claim of expert tactical balance follows from it.
  • Harness limitation: tool latency makes timed battles a poor measure of human reaction difficulty. Some instantaneous taps were rejected by the UI’s intentional minimum hold; these were corrected with delayed presses. They are not reported as touch bugs.
  • Coverage limit: mobile was 390×844 Chromium emulation; desktop was 1440×900. No physical phone, Galaxy A9 thermal run, human user study, full manual late-game reign or accessibility certification was performed.
  • Errors: no game page/console errors were recorded in the completed play and control logs. The installed game skill client also completed two screenshot/state iterations.

Rubric, weights, confidence and reasons for every grade

Scale: 0–2 absent or obstructive; 3–4 weak; 5–6 functional but inconsistent; 7–8 strong; 9–10 exceptional and well supported. Product bands: below 40 D, 40–54 C−, 55–69 C, 70–79 B, 80–89 A−, 90–100 A. These are review conventions, not industry standards.

Calculation: platform total = Σ(score out of 10 × weight) ÷ 10. Each platform’s weights sum to 100. Mobile weighs clarity, learning and pacing more heavily; desktop weighs strategy, economy, territory and combat more heavily. Combined averages the two totals. Confidence describes evidence strength, not a statistical interval.

Meaningful strategic choices — mobile 7, desktop 7 /10. Medium confidence. Doctrines, claims, hero appointments and cards have consequences. Engaged automation survives almost twice as many waves as declining; this does not establish several equally viable expert plans.

Economy rewards mastery — mobile 5.5, desktop 5.5 /10. Medium confidence. Terrain, focus, governors, logistics and markets interact. Extra economic activity produced much more gold but only a small, noisy survival improvement in this probe.

Territory and logistics — mobile 6.5, desktop 7 /10. Medium confidence. Routes, supply connections, loyalty and military travel already matter. The interface could make route value, arrival time and opportunity cost easier to compare.

Tactical combat — mobile 6.5, desktop 7 /10. Medium confidence. Five formations, stances, stamina, moments, withdrawal and command delegation create a promising decision space. Late escalation also shortens reading windows and removes help.

Clarity and feedback — mobile 5, desktop 5.5 /10. High confidence. Strong art and useful aftermath coexist with a composite POWER beside a different THREAT quantity, mixed progression labels and a confirmed “certain”/53% contradiction.

First-run learning — mobile 4.5, desktop 5 /10. Medium confidence. Rich identity creation precedes the strategic hook; an empty inheritance sheet still appears on the first reign. A quick coronation path and contextual Copilot already exist.

Pacing and attention — mobile 5.5, desktop 6 /10. Medium confidence. The court and combat have useful rhythm, but the played opening repeatedly interrupted preparation. Desktop Hands-on suppresses routine prompts; that changes pacing as well as control.

Progression and reward — mobile 6.5, desktop 6.5 /10. Medium confidence. Legacy, Dynasty and Cabinet give continuity. Their overlapping levels, duplicates and loadouts make it difficult to tell which reward changes this run.

Replay and satisfying endings — mobile 5.5, desktop 5.5 /10. Medium confidence. Seeds, heroes, cards, stories and waves provide variety. Main Ascent is endless, with defeat and inheritance rather than a selectable campaign victory contract.

Platform controls — mobile 6.5, desktop 7.5 /10. Medium confidence. Phone controls use a compact dock; desktop has a map with side sheets, keys and manual orders. Stable shortcuts, comparisons and measured touch ergonomics can improve both.

Identity and presentation — mobile 9, desktop 9 /10. High confidence. Vietnamese history, named characters and Đông Hồ print art give a coherent identity worth preserving. This is the clearest product differentiator.

Accessibility and interruption comfort — mobile 4.5, desktop 5 /10. Medium confidence. Save/resume and pauses exist. Late-game assistance overrides and small combat annotations are concrete concerns; physical-device performance and assistive access remain unverified.

Commercial fit, monetization quality, multiplayer and physical-device stability are not graded because this review does not establish them. Accessibility deductions reflect observed design constraints, not an unsupported claim of standards noncompliance.

Release judgment: keep developing the current core. Prioritize truthful decisions, consistent comfort settings and one finite playable charter before expanding map size, currencies or unit count. A high art score is a reason to protect the identity, not a reason to postpone usability work.

For mobile fun

A player can understand the immediate problem, make a consequential choice, see its result and stop at a satisfying boundary. Low action count should reduce handling effort while preserving the need to choose.

This synthesis is an inference from the described designs and the local play review—not a market-wide user survey.

For desktop depth

Experts should win by anticipating routes, managing commitments, exploiting interactions and responding to uncertain situations. More control should offer better plans, comparisons and execution—not compulsory maintenance clicks.

Vạn Thắng can retain one simulation and expose different planning surfaces. Shared rules make balance and teaching easier to reason about.

Commercial context, accessed 12 September 2026: the English-language Steam review summaries observed for Thronefall, Against the Storm and Polytopia were each 95% positive. Review populations and dates differ. This is directional evidence of receptive audiences for these products, not proof of revenue, mobile success or causation by any single mechanic. See M1 · Thronefall, M5 · Against the Storm and M6 · The Battle of Polytopia.

06 / SIMULATION & BALANCE

Participation matters. The value of deeper economic play is less clear.

64 runs: basic decision agency

16 seeds × four policies; fresh profile before each run; 600-tick cap. Mean waves survived:

Engaged
21.4
Random
17.2
Declining
10.9
Contrarian
10.0

Engaged choices achieved 1.95× declining’s survival. That supports real consequences. It does not demonstrate that sophisticated planning beats merely accepting available options.

All 64 ended in defeat before the cap. These policies resolve choices programmatically and do not reproduce human reading time or desktop Hands-on play.

48 runs: economic activity

A separate economy harness; 16 seeds × three policies, also fresh per run.

PolicyWavesPeak gold
engaged18.54,529
focused19.17,180
steward20.216,456

Steward produced about 3.6× the mean peak gold of Engaged, but only about 9% more waves. Much more handling did not yet demonstrate a reliable survival advantage.

“Engaged” is implemented differently in these two harnesses; compare policies within each experiment, not the 18.5 and 21.4 baselines across them.

Uncertainty and reproducibility of the economy result

The approximate paired-seed 95% t intervals for additional waves are focused: 0.56 [-4.88, 6.01]; steward: 1.69 [-3.60, 6.97]. Both include zero. These 16-seed samples do not establish a reliable improvement or prove that economic planning is useless.

Policies can consume random draws in different orders, so matching world seeds does not hold every later combat event identical. The next experiment should separate world generation, strategic events and battle RNG streams, then compare both outcomes and investment timing. Also examine whether extra gold was spent productively, became a late stockpile, or was earned only after an earlier advantage.

The t intervals summarize this small sample; they are not a causal confidence claim. Raw trajectories, purchase histories and the calculation are in economy-fresh-profile.json and economy-summary.json.

83.9/85 is a proxy score, not a “98.7% fun” rating.

The repository metric rewards policy separation, variable pacing, escalating threat, scarce purchasing power and battle appearances. Several dimensions saturate easily. A maximum threat/defence ratio near 19× earns full tension marks; a battle appearing 12.8 times earns full showpiece marks even though the printed target is 3–5. Neither checks whether the player felt capable, informed or fatigued.

Current proxyWhat it cannot establishBetter companion measure
Engaged / declining ratioSeveral competent strategies are viable; choices demand learning.Adaptive expert policies, ablations and map-dependent dominance.
Decision-gap variancePauses feel well paced; interruptions are welcome.Wall-clock reading time, modal count, abandoned tasks and player recall.
Peak threat / defenceTension is recoverable rather than hopeless.Time in a recoverable state, counterplay availability and loss explanation.
Peak treasury / dearest offerPurchases are useful, timely and affordable at the relevant moment.Actionable purchasing power and marginal return at the time of commitment.
Battle screen appearancesEach fight asks a different question or remains enjoyable.Distinct tactical situations, manual/delegated choice and fatigue by run length.

Three balance mechanisms deserve measurement before redesign.

  1. Wave response to growth. The target combines a rising base curve, ambition, rival pressure and bounded/lagged responses to defensive strength. The player-match factor has a free lead threshold and a cap; it does not cancel every power gain. Test the marginal benefit of a prepared wall or host, then expose a concise committed forecast.
  2. Income and wealth scaling. Current prices respond to both the economic rate and excess stores. Older design notes describing income-only scaling are stale. Show how long a purchase takes to repay and whether a saved reserve is still meaningful; avoid reflexively deleting every anti-snowball rule.
  3. Attention as a hidden cost. Steward’s mean activity included roughly 21 focus changes, four governor postings, 14 manual claims and 128 sales. An action-heavy policy can win slightly more while being much less pleasant. Measure benefit per meaningful decision, not raw clicks.

The original shared-profile 64-run probe was retained only as a diagnostic. Fresh-profile reruns are the basis of the headline results. Evidence: metrics; metric implementation; wave director; current tuning constants.

07 / IDEA → CRITICISM → TUNING → RECHECK

Nine proposals, refined through two critiques.

These loops are design reasoning informed by the current implementation and test evidence. They are not fabricated user-test rounds. Each ends with a smaller implementable direction and a criterion that could reject it.

01 · Keep combat readable as mastery rises

Add more speed and hide the counter guide in late waves, so experienced players must react and remember.

The current game already does this. Wave 13 enforces fast pace; later steps cap speech, raise enemy difficulty and hide assistance. Success can make the interface less accessible. Memorizing a ring is a different skill from choosing when to spend stamina.

Separate enemy competence, combat speed and reading assistance. Retain the player’s slow pace, explicit counter guide and optional automatic pause at a decision.

Unlimited stopping could remove time pressure for players who enjoy it. A globally slower battle could also make ordinary fights drag.

Ship independent settings: enemy difficulty, pace, readable intent, and pause-on-moment. Keep a clearly chosen timed challenge preset. Use stronger enemy plans and fewer safe responses to raise strategic difficulty; preserve assistance in normal runs.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: At wave 20+, the selected slow speed and guide remain effective. In usability tests, at least 80% can explain the next enemy action before choosing a response. Treat that percentage as a target to test, not an existing result.

Backlog links: B02, B03, B04

02 · A reign should sometimes end in triumph

Add a victory at wave 12, then end every run.

A mandatory cutoff would truncate a strong build. A fixed wave count also treats exploration, diplomacy and defence as the same achievement.

Offer a finite charter with a wave horizon and one thematic goal, followed by a choice to bank the result or continue.

Stacking several objectives can turn a relaxing phone run into a checklist. Banking too early may become the optimal progression farm.

Prototype one short charter: hold the capital through the first great invasion and preserve one chosen border. The initial candidate is the first four waves, tuned by observed wall-clock sessions. Award a complete ending; offer a second chapter or Endless. Later charters can emphasize trade or alliances. Normalize rewards by difficulty and meaningful milestones.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: Candidate mobile chapter: 8–12 minutes including reading; desktop extended reign: 20–35 minutes. These are hypotheses. Keep only if players understand the goal and at least 70% of finishers want another chapter or a new build.

Backlog links: B12, B13, B14

03 · Preparation needs uninterrupted space

Remove most court cards and let autopilot handle the economy.

Cards are currently the main way many phone players exercise agency. Removing them would turn a grand strategy game into watching the simulation.

Queue routine advice in a compact court inbox; interrupt for danger, an expiring commitment or a genuinely new rule.

An inbox can become an invisible backlog. Too much batching can make all strategy happen in one exhausting menu.

Use the existing Aftermath → Court → Muster → Field structure. Present one strategic headline and up to three optional queued decisions. Pause for urgent, irreversible choices. Allow the player to pull any lane on demand. Let doctrine handle repeat maintenance under visible reserve budgets.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: Target no more than two unsolicited full-screen decisions between ordinary waves after onboarding. Measure decision comprehension, ignored important events and actions per completed objective—not simply fewer taps.

Backlog links: B08, B09, B18

04 · Make growth feel like an advantage

Remove all enemy adaptation and all price scaling.

The current game uses several bounded controllers, not a single unlimited rubber band. Removing everything could produce idle snowballs and trivial late-game purchases.

Publish the base wave, ambition, rival pressure and adaptive portion; lock a visible wave budget before the player finishes preparing.

A player may exploit the lock by hoarding strength until after the snapshot. Full formulas on a phone would be unreadable.

First instrument each contribution and run matched policy experiments. Prototype a muster snapshot with a bounded adaptation envelope. Count committed recruitment and construction when appropriate. Keep a short front forecast with a detail drill-down. Demand a measurable benefit from successful preparation before retuning all prices.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: On the same scenario, a sensible defensive investment should improve losses, territory held or capital safety in a large majority of cases. Pre-register an 80% directional target and inspect exceptions. Compare outcomes as well as the displayed POWER.

Backlog links: B10, B15, B16, B17

05 · Build identity from interactions

Add dozens of new cards, units and building levels.

There are already 52 card definitions, 22 eligible for normal drafts and eight opening boons. More content may dilute the chance of forming a coherent plan and multiply balance work.

Audit the existing pool for three viable engines: fortified food/logistics, trading diplomacy, and mobile expansion. Give each a visible strength and a failure case.

Rigid engines could make drafts solved recipes; forced card bundles would reduce improvisation.

Keep flexible bridges between engines. Prototype two interaction changes within the existing pool before expanding it. A food surplus might support a reserve host but face wage pressure; trade can fund defence but needs safe connections; expansion opens resources but stretches supply. Clearly mark proposed interactions that do not exist yet.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: Across 32–64 seeds and several competent policies, no starter engine should dominate every map. Players should name their build and its weakness after the second draft. Rework generic upgrades that cannot change a decision.

Backlog links: B20, B21, B22, B23

06 · One simulation, two comfortable ways to command

Give desktop players more compulsory micromanagement than mobile players.

Desktop already starts with Hands-on enabled, disabling autopilot and routine lane prompts. More chores are not automatically more depth, and platform defaults can conceal that this is a rules change.

Share the economic and combat rules. Let players choose Guided command or Hands-on command on either platform, with clear explanations and easy switching.

An expert workspace can overwhelm a phone; automation must not silently override explicit orders or make experts irrelevant.

Mobile uses intent presets, single-province drill-down and one urgent front at a time. Desktop adds pinned comparisons, stable shortcuts, routes, queues and optional multi-host selection. Both expose reserve budgets, order precedence and the same consequences. Prototype the command workspace with existing armies before adding units.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: A desktop player can compare two fronts and queue a response in under 20 seconds after learning the controls. A mobile player can give an equivalent strategic intention in at most three major taps. Validate, do not assume, both targets.

Backlog links: B07, B18, B24, B25, B26

07 · Make inheritance rewarding without obscuring skill

Merge Legacy, Dynasty and Cabinet into one universal currency.

A hard merge would discard distinct rewards and disrupt existing saves. Removing progression power overnight could make earned collections feel devalued.

Unify the explanation and end-of-run presentation while keeping the underlying stores. Distinguish permanent collection level, this-run stack and current-reign experience.

A prettier reward screen alone does not resolve grinding or fresh-profile disadvantage.

Use one inheritance summary: what was earned, what changed, and one optional next-run choice. Add a normalized challenge preset with clearly defined progression treatment. Prefer new options and sidegrades for future rewards; preserve existing ownership and test any balance migration separately.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: At least 80% of testers can identify which of three rewards affects the next run, this run or collection completion. Compare new and progressed profiles with identical decision policies.

Backlog links: B05, B19, B30, B31

08 · Turn defeat into a useful next attempt

Add a detailed log explaining every multiplier after a loss.

There is already an aftermath and chronicle. A huge ledger may explain the engine while failing to help a disappointed player decide what to try next.

Show the decisive timeline: arrival, supply failure, formation exchange, reinforcement or capital loss. Offer one plausible alternative with an uncertainty label.

A counterfactual can be wrong when changing an order changes later random events. Automatic advice can sound falsely certain or blame the player.

Start with facts from the event log: “Relief arrived two seasons after contact.” Add a bounded comparison only where it can be simulated consistently. Let players replay a practice snapshot when feasible. Lead with the story and one learnable cause; keep the detailed ledger optional.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: After a loss, at least 70% can name one specific adjustment for the next attempt. Verify every factual explanation against recorded events. Do not fabricate precise alternate win chances.

Backlog links: B11, B27, B28

09 · Make Vietnamese strategy part of the rules

Build a full naval layer, historical campaign map and many new factions immediately.

That scope would compete with the current game’s clarity and balance problems. New movement, combat and economy layers would require extensive teaching and art.

Use existing formations, terrain, supply and character stories for a small historical scenario with a distinct tactical problem.

A famous battle becomes a trivia skin if the winning action is unchanged; a scripted historical win can remove agency.

Prototype one river-crossing or prepared-ground encounter. Telegraph its rule, allow more than one solution, and make a retreat/bait plan costly if mistimed. Keep historical framing separate from invented procedural outcomes. Expand only if this encounter changes players’ decisions and remains legible on a phone.

Next loop / keep-or-reject test: Players should describe the scenario’s terrain rule without opening a codex and use at least two successful approaches. Reuse existing systems before introducing a full navy.

Backlog links: B29, B34, B35

08 / MOBILE FUN + DESKTOP DEPTH

Share the rules. Adapt the planning surface.

DecisionMobile presentationDesktop presentationShared depth
Prepare a borderOne forecast card; tap Hold border, Reinforce or Negotiate.Pin two fronts; inspect ETA, garrison, routes and economic cost before queueing orders.Same terrain, supplies, travel and enemy plan.
Run the economyChoose a doctrine and reserve budget; review exceptions.Compare province output, governors and build queues; override any district.Same prices, upkeep and resource bottlenecks.
Fight a battleReadable intent, thumb-sized formations, optional decision pause and commander delegation.Stable formation/stance keys, front switching, detailed combat log and optional challenge timing.Same formation matchups, reform risk and stamina.

Example: one hard decision, two comfortable interfaces

An army reaches the rice border in three seasons; relief needs four. A mobile card offers hold with the levy, withdraw and preserve the host, or pay for a delaying agreement, with cost and expected consequences. Desktop shows the same options alongside route and province comparisons. Both players choose what to sacrifice. Neither needs to issue a hundred soldier orders.

This is a proposed scenario, not a claim that these exact three actions are currently available together. The existing supply, standing-order, diplomacy and withdrawal systems provide the foundations.

For touch, audit actual hit regions and spacing. Apple recommends at least 44 × 44 points; W3C’s enhanced target guidance uses 44 × 44 CSS pixels. These units are not interchangeable across native shells and device scaling. Start with a 44 CSS-pixel web target where feasible, then verify physical-device ergonomics and platform conventions. M8 · Apple; M9 · W3C.

09 / IMPLEMENTATION INVENTORY

48 changes, extensions and deliberate deferrals.

This is the complete prioritized inventory from the reviewed product scope—not every feature a grand-strategy game could conceivably contain. Improve means the system exists; Extend adds capability to it; New means no player-facing implementation was found in the inspected main flow; Validate requires evidence first; Defer means do not build yet.

P0: trust, measurement or a blocking usability issue. P1: next playable milestone. P2: depth and polish after proof. P3: defer. Effort S/M/L/XL is relative engineering/design scope, not a delivery estimate; asset work and save migration can change it.

10 / WHAT TO BUILD FIRST

Three playable milestones, each with a stop gate.

Milestone 1 / Trust & control

Readable preparation and battle

  • Fix certainty copy, empty inheritance and resume overlap.
  • Keep pace and assistance settings effective.
  • Explain command modes; stabilize pause and shortcuts.
  • Capture comparable front forecasts and clean experiment metadata.

Gate: players understand a choice and can control the clock. Stop expanding content if this still fails.

Core: B01–B07, B10–B11, B24. Start device/text audits in parallel with implementation work.

Milestone 2 / A complete session

One charter worth replaying

  • Ship one finite objective with bank/continue.
  • Use wave phases to budget interruptions.
  • Add a practical resource/arrival forecast.
  • Make inheritance and a loss’s decisive cause clear.

Gate: people finish or lose with understanding, and voluntarily choose another attempt. Do not multiply charters before this works.

Core: B08–B09, B12–B19, B27, B30.

Milestone 3 / Earned mastery

Three plans and expert tools

  • Tune three viable engines using existing cards.
  • Add desktop comparisons and mobile intent commands.
  • Prototype one terrain/historical encounter.
  • Offer normalized challenges after profile tests.

Gate: multiple plans succeed for different reasons, without more compulsory taps or a universal best build.

Core: B20–B26, B29, B31, B34–B35.

The first implementation batch should be small and reviewable.

  1. Correct decision promises. Start in ascent localization and the conquest-method presenter/resolver. Use shared probability data rather than independent prose.
  2. Separate comfort from escalation. Review ASCENT_BATTLE_ESCALATION and the battle-options code. Preserve selected pace and readable guidance; test late waves directly.
  3. Remove empty opening steps and fix resume layout. Keep the existing coronation shortcut and returning-house ceremony. Use the captured first-run and resume screenshots as concrete cases.
  4. Make mode and pause behavior explicit. Update normal run entry and keyboard handling without changing the underlying simulation balance.
  5. Replace one misleading forecast. Add defence ready by contact beside an incoming front. Include its source components in telemetry before changing the wave curve.

No game mechanic changes were made for this review. Sequencing is a planning recommendation, not a promised schedule. Estimate each milestone after inspecting its implementation and save-compatibility requirements.

11 / VALIDATION PLAN

Test whether the player understands, chooses and wants another reign.

Use short evidence loops after each milestone. The thresholds below are proposed decision gates, not results from the current review. Avoid using a larger simulation score as the only shipping criterion.

1. First-run comprehension and attention

Sample: begin with 8–12 people, split between mobile-first strategy players and experienced desktop strategy players. Treat this as qualitative discovery, not statistically representative market research. Observe a fresh profile without coaching.

Capture: time to the first consequential choice; time to the first understandable consequence; modal interruptions; missed costs; voluntary delegation; pause use; the reason for quitting. Candidate goals: first strategic choice within 60 seconds on the quick path, ≥80% correctly explain three of four representative choices, and ≥70% can name an adjustment after defeat. Revise the UI when people fail for the same reason.

2. Balance without hiding the profile

Matrix: 32–64 world seeds × fresh/progressed profile × Guided/Hands-on × three competent plans. Use separate random streams for map, events and battle where possible. Report uncertainty and early/late outcomes; record the exact version, selected perks and cabinet levels.

Capture: charter completion, waves, land retained, friendly losses, capital safety, spendable reserves and decision count. Test one ablation at a time: income/wealth scaling, adaptation envelope, automation reserves and draft interactions. Do not reward deliberate refusal or stockpiling with a misleading “expert” label.

3. Tactical depth rather than memory alone

Compare competent counterplay, fixed formation, good retreat timing and commander delegation in the same battle scenarios. Vary army composition, terrain and supplies. Log reform exposure, stamina spent, moments answered and losses.

Gate: a readable opponent should remain challenging through its plan and tradeoffs. Preserve the slow setting and guide in ordinary late-game play. Ensure no formation or stance wins almost everywhere, and no single human-speed timing target is imposed on all players.

4. Charter length and replay desire

Test the four-wave short charter against the existing opening, with equal content quality. Measure wall-clock length including reading, completion/abandonment, whether the ending felt earned, and whether the player chooses another chapter or a different build.

Gate: evaluate the 8–12 minute mobile and 20–35 minute extended desktop hypotheses. Do not force a target duration by stripping the choices people enjoyed. Watch for repeat farming of the shortest reward path.

5. Physical-device reliability

Use at least a lower-end Android phone/tablet and a representative iPhone, plus desktop keyboard/mouse. Test a sustained 20-minute run, dense combat, large text, repeated pause/resume and interruption while a choice is open.

Candidate performance budget: a stable 30 FPS mode on the declared low-end target, with frame-time distribution, input latency, memory and thermal behavior recorded. Report p95 frame time against 33.3 ms rather than only average FPS. Test offline restore and pending rewards for duplication or loss. This review does not certify those budgets.

Reproduce the review probes

Start the development server with npm run dev on port 5179. The review’s fresh-profile copies are included in the evidence folder; each clears only its isolated test browser’s local storage before booting a new simulated state. Run these commands from the repository root with its dependencies installed. The original harnesses remain unchanged.

node docs/phase-2/gameplay-review-2026-09-12/evidence/review-fresh-metrics.mjs --seeds 16 --ticks 600 --json

node docs/phase-2/gameplay-review-2026-09-12/evidence/review-fresh-economy.mjs --seeds 16 --ticks 600 --policies engaged,focused,steward --json docs/phase-2/gameplay-review-2026-09-12/evidence/economy-fresh-profile.json --quiet

node docs/phase-2/gameplay-review-2026-09-12/evidence/review-combat.mjs

The included drivers import the repository’s existing playtest helpers. Future changes to those helpers or game source can change the results; retain the recorded revision and raw evidence. A reviewed profile-isolation option should ultimately live in the shared harness. This HTML embeds all displayed screenshots and interactive data; local evidence/code links additionally require the accompanying repository folder.

Prepared for the current game, with implementation recommendations rather than gameplay changes. Read the verdict, choose a milestone, implement the smallest testable slice, criticize the result, and repeat.
